newsitem.title: USA: U.S. high court dismisses line-item veto challenge.
newsitem.headline: U.S. high court dismisses line-item veto challenge.

text.p: The Supreme Court Thursday stopped short of deciding the constitutionality of a law giving the president new power to veto individual spending and tax items, dismissing a challenge to the law on technical grounds.
The high court ruled by a 7-2 vote that the six members of Congress who sued in challenging the historic line-item veto law lacked the legal standing or right to bring the case in the first place.
President Clinton has yet to use his expanded veto power under the law, which took effect in January. A U.S. District Court judge earlier this year struck down the law as unconstitutional.

Clinton administration lawyers appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing the lawmakers lacked standing to bring the case. But if the court decided to reach the merits of the dispute, then it should uphold the law as constitutional, they said.

"We hold that (the lawmakers) lack standing to bring this suit and therefore direct that the judgment of the district court be vacated and the complaint dismissed," Chief Justice William Rehnquist declared for the court majority.

One of the two dissenters, Justice John Paul Stevens, said he would declare the law unconstitutional. The law allows the president to strip items from spending measures without vetoing the entire bill.
